accuracy.evidence: Curriculum terms checked against the English National Curriculum programmes of study (Year 1 and Year 2 writing composition: writing for different purposes including non-fiction, sequencing sentences to form short narratives and texts) and US Common Core W.K.2 and W.1.2 (informative/explanatory texts that name a topic, supply some facts and provide some sense of closure). Every fact in the lab is true: butterflies are insects with wings, antennae, a body and six legs (drawn as three per side); frogs lay frogspawn and tadpoles grow into frogs; honey bees make honey and live in hives; bees have six legs.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early non-fiction slips: drifting into story ('Once upon a time there was a butterfly' is refused with the reason), treating opinions as facts ('I think frogs are cute', 'Frogs are the best!'), keeping made-up details ('My frog can fly a kite'), off-topic sentences about the writer's day ('I had pizza for tea'), ending with 'The end.' (refused in the build step) and labels pointing to the wrong part.

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanism is the shape of an information text: opening sentences that name a topic, a fact/not-fact sort, an off-topic cut on two pages, a butterfly diagram with leader lines to label, and a page that only accepts heading, topic sentence, facts and closing in that order and rejects 'The end.'. It differs from flagtopic (finding the main topic of a text someone else wrote), flagfvo (fact vs opinion for older readers) and flagtale (story beginning and ending); the 30% shingle gate passed against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers the structure by building it: picking 'Once upon a time' gets 'starts a story. Information starts by naming the topic'; dropping 'Tadpoles grow into frogs' in Not a fact gets 'That is true for frogs, so it is a fact'; tapping the closing card before the facts gets 'The closing sentence goes last'. The step summaries only confirm what the taps showed.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: '"Once upon a time…"' as an opening is disproved in the first step; 'Yes, it is about frogs' for 'I think frogs are cute' is disproved by the fact sort; '"The end."' as an ending is disproved when that card is refused in the build step.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with twelve tagged messages naming the slip: story opening, off-topic opening, 'the best' as opinion, made-up singing cow, keeping a train fact as if off-topic (two variants), 'The end.', 'Once upon a time' as an ending, heading at the bottom or in the middle, a label on the ear, and a label pointing anywhere.

readability.evidence: Kid text reads at FK 1.6 with short sentences and concrete examples (frogs, bees, labels); canvas sentences are four to seven words; every action has a 56 px young-class button. Adult text reads at FK 5.9 and uses the exact terms writing for different purposes, non-fiction, sequence sentences, informative/explanatory texts, name a topic, supply some facts and sense of closure.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler patterns and the 12% duplicate gate (including Main Topic of Informational Texts and Fact vs opinion). Each kid paragraph adds one step of the text type (facts not story, name the topic, facts only and stay on topic, labels and closing); adult paragraphs give the curriculum statements, the parts of the text, common mistakes and the lab outline.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px Android light and iPhone 13 dark screenshots of all six steps: the picture and sentence slot, the frog card with both bins, the four sentence rows on the bee page, the butterfly with four numbered label boxes and leader lines, and the page frame all fit with nothing clipped; long sentence buttons wrap. phone_sweep reported 0 findings.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: every task completes with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge shows, axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in light and dark themes, no console errors. Every drag or canvas tap has a button route (sentence buttons, Fact / Not a fact, a button per row, Box 1 to 4 with aria-labels naming the label, a button per page card) and the canvas aria-label announces each result.

sources: Department for Education (2013), English programmes of study: key stage 1, Year 1 and Year 2 writing composition (statutory requirements and notes)
Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts, W.K.2 and W.1.2 (informative/explanatory texts)
Natural History Museum: butterfly anatomy (head with antennae, thorax with six legs and four wings, abdomen)
RSPB / Froglife: common frog life cycle (frogspawn, tadpoles, froglets)
British Beekeepers Association: honey bee colony and hive basics
